newsitem.title: Albania: Albania protesters occupy port for second day.
newsitem.headline: Albania protesters occupy port for second day.

text.p: Thousands of angry Albanians surged through this port city for the second day running blaming president Sali Berisha for the collapse of pyramid investment schemes that has left them penniless.

Token cordons of riot police were overwhelmed by 30,000 protesters who poured through the streets towards Independence Square by mid-morning, their ranks swelled by villagers who had lost life savings in the failed schemes.

"Vlore is ours, down with the government," the crowd chanted, punching the air and demanding the resignation of Berisha's right-wing government. "Sali, you thief, where have you put our money?" others shouted.

At least 10,000 moved on to the main police station to demand -- and win -- the release of 20 protesters detained after a day of skirmishes with police on Wednesday. Protesters pelted police briefly with stones in the day's only violence.
Even more massed again in the evening on a darkened palm-lined boulevard, many carrying candles or torches made from large pieces of paper set alight.
Children and elderly women strode alongside their menfolk as a call from a mosque marked the end of the day's fast for Ramadan. Not a single government or opposition politician was in sight.
"We want, we want, we want our money," chanted the marchers as they moved off to the harbour and back again.
"They've threatened us all with arrest. Maybe they'll arrest me," said Ilir, a man in his late twenties. "I've lost all my money. I live in a tent. Better prison than a tent."
In the capital Tirana, the Interior Ministry denounced the confrontation outside the police station, blamed "extremist and terrorist elements" and urged city residents to disown them.

The new protests, so far confined to Vlore, were sparked by the collapse of the Gjallica investment scheme, hugely popular in the region. They were the first since angry depositors set fire to public buildings in several cities last month.
More than 150 people were arrested after those disturbances and face minimum 15-year jail terms on public order charges.
On Wednesday, police fought pitched battles with demonstrators through streets littered with shattered glass, but twice failed to disperse them.
The interior ministry said three demonstrators and three policemen were injured in Wednesday's clashes. The country's most popular newspaper, Koha Jone, said 20 people were hurt.

Berisha has made no public appearance since Tuesday, when he held talks on the crisis boycotted by the Socialist-led opposition. He then offered limited help to ruined depositors, particularly those who had sold homes to increase their stake.
In an interview published on Thursday he said his opponents had failed in their aim of turning discontent into a bloodbath.
"The opposition made a big mistake. It wanted a bloodbath and it did not happen," Berisha told the Paris daily Le Monde. "Albania is calm."
Virtually every family has invested money in the schemes in the six years since Albania emerged from eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime.
Partial refunds are being dispensed for two failed pyramid schemes but many depositors are angry at not getting their entire stake back.
Some accuse the ruling Democratic Party, founded by Berisha, of using the proceeds to finance its re-election in polls last year, denounced as rigged by Western observers.
Gjallica owed depositors an estimated $500 million and was the fifth major pyramid scheme to go bankrupt since November.
A small number of other investment schemes are clinging to life, although they have cut interest payments. Economists believe as much as $2 billion was tied up altogether.
